title: Foundations of U.S. History
in30Seconds: United States history runs from the many peoples living in the Americas before European contact, through colonization, revolution, expansion and slavery, civil war, industrialization, and the rise of a world power. Running through it is one hard tension: founding ideals of liberty and equality set against realities that denied them to enslaved people, Native nations, and women. This lesson is a map, not the territory, and hands each era to its own topic.
whyItMatters: Almost every specific U.S. topic makes more sense once you can place it on the arc and see the questions that recur across it: who counts as fully free and equal, and who decides. Holding the founding ideals and the injustices of the same era together, rather than picking one, is what separates an honest account from a comforting or a cynical one. The skills you practice here, weighing sources and perspectives and telling facts from interpretation, are the same ones you will use on every era that follows and on the arguments about American history happening right now.
learningObjectives: Outline the broad arc and rough periodization of U.S. history from Indigenous America through the 20th century, treating the era boundaries as conventions.
Explain the central tension between the nation's founding ideals and the historical realities that contradicted them.
Describe U.S. history as the interaction of diverse peoples and as an ongoing struggle to extend rights.
Apply basic historical-thinking skills and multiple perspectives to distinguish established facts from interpretation.

collegeVersion.heading: The arc, as a rough map
collegeVersion.body: It helps to carry a rough sequence of eras for U.S. history, as long as you remember it is a convenience, not a law of nature. A common ordering runs: the many Indigenous nations living across the Americas long before 1492; European colonization from the sixteenth century onward; the Revolution and the founding of a new republic in the 1770s and 1780s; westward expansion and the deepening of slavery across the first half of the nineteenth century; the Civil War and Reconstruction in the 1860s and 1870s; rapid industrialization, urban growth, and mass immigration through the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; and the emergence of the United States as a global power across the twentieth century. Each of these is a whole topic in its own right, and this lesson only names them so you can see how they connect. The boundaries are contested: historians argue about where one era ends and the next begins, and any scheme that starts the story in 1492 or 1776 risks treating tens of thousands of years of Indigenous history as a mere prelude. Hold the map loosely.

collegeVersion.heading: Ideals and realities, held together
collegeVersion.body: The Declaration of Independence, adopted in Congress on July 4, 1776, put a set of ideals at the center of the new nation's self-understanding: that 'all men are created equal,' that they hold 'unalienable Rights' including 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness,' and that a just government draws its authority from 'the consent of the governed.' Those words were genuinely radical, and they have been quoted by reformers ever since. Yet the same society that produced them denied them to millions. Slavery was legal throughout the new nation, and the enslaved population grew from roughly 700,000 people at the first census in 1790 to nearly four million by 1860. Native nations were pushed off their land through war, treaty-breaking, and forced removal. Women could not vote and lost many legal rights in marriage, and free Black Americans faced deep discrimination even where they were not enslaved. The honest move is not to choose between the ideals and the injustices, nor to let one excuse the other. Both are true at once, and the distance between them is not a footnote to U.S. history. It is one of its main subjects, and much of what follows is a long, contested argument over who the words 'all men' actually include.

collegeVersion.heading: A history of many peoples and ongoing struggles
collegeVersion.body: U.S. history is not the story of one group acting while others watch. The Americas before European arrival held millions of people in numerous and sophisticated societies, and the history that followed was made by the interaction of Native American, European, and African peoples, later joined by successive waves of immigrants from around the world. Europeans came to dominate, but that dominance was built on Native land and on the coerced labor of enslaved Africans, and it never erased the peoples it displaced. Read this way, much of U.S. history becomes a series of struggles to extend the founding promise to people first left out of it: enslaved people who freed themselves and pressed for emancipation and citizenship, Native nations defending their sovereignty, women organizing for the vote and legal equality, workers, immigrants, and many others. Progress in these struggles was real but uneven, contested, and sometimes reversed. Seeing the nation's diversity and these ongoing struggles is not a side theme added for balance; it is what the arc is actually made of.

collegeVersion.heading: Studying it critically
collegeVersion.body: Because history is argued, not just remembered, you study it with a small set of habits rather than by trusting the first account you meet. Sourcing means asking who created a document or account, when, and why, before deciding how much to trust it. Contextualization means placing a source in its own time instead of judging it only by today's assumptions, while still describing historical harm accurately. Corroboration means comparing several sources and noticing where they agree and clash. Close reading means attending to exactly what a source claims and what evidence it offers. Above all, keep separating two different things: established facts, meaning what happened and when, which good evidence can settle, from interpretation, meaning why it happened and what it meant, where thoughtful historians using the same facts can reasonably disagree. Weighing multiple perspectives, including those of the colonized, the enslaved, and the excluded, is not a way of avoiding the truth. It is how you get closer to it.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of dividing the past into named eras or periods; a useful convention for organizing history, not a fixed feature of the past itself.
The principles the new United States claimed for itself, chiefly liberty, equality, and government by consent, most famously stated in the Declaration of Independence.
The 1776 document, adopted July 4, in which the colonies declared separation from Britain and asserted that all men are created equal and hold unalienable rights.
The idea that a government's legitimate authority comes from the agreement of the people it rules, rather than from inheritance or force.
The process by which Native nations were deprived of their land and sovereignty through war, coerced treaties, and forced removal.
A set of analytic skills, including sourcing, contextualization, corroboration, and close reading, used to interpret evidence about the past rather than simply memorize it.
The distinction between what happened and when, which evidence can establish, and why it happened and what it meant, where historians may reasonably differ.
The era after the Civil War, roughly 1865 to 1877, when the nation debated and partly attempted to rebuild the South and extend rights to formerly enslaved people.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of U.S. history as a long road with big milestones: peoples already living here, colonies arriving, a break from Britain, a country spreading west while holding people in slavery, a civil war over that, factories and newcomers, and then a world power. This lesson is the road map, and other lessons are the actual stops. The tricky part to keep in your head is that the country wrote down beautiful promises, that everyone is equal and free, at the very same time it broke those promises for a lot of people. Both facts are real. Good history means holding them together and asking careful questions about who said what, and why, instead of just believing the first story you hear.
eli10.analogy: It is like the founding rules of a club that say every member is equal, written by people who then quietly barred most of the town from joining. The rules still matter, because later people point to them and say, you wrote 'everyone,' so let us in. Much of the club's later history is that argument playing out.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy is too gentle. Exclusion from U.S. rights was not a quiet oversight but was enforced through slavery, war, and law, with lasting harm; and a nation is not a club you can simply leave, so the stakes and the suffering were far greater than any membership dispute.

workedExample: Take one sentence: 'The Declaration of Independence made Americans equal.' Run it through historical thinking. Sourcing: the Declaration was written in 1776 by elite colonists making a political case for independence, not a law guaranteeing rights. Contextualization: in 1776 slavery was legal in every one of the colonies, and women and unpropertied men could not vote. Corroboration: census records show roughly 700,000 enslaved people in 1790, and other sources document Native dispossession and women's legal disabilities. Close reading: the text says people 'are created equal' and 'ought to be' free, an aspiration, not a description of the society. Revised claim: the Declaration announced an ideal of equality that the nation did not extend to most people at the time, and that later movements used to demand inclusion. That revised sentence is one you can defend.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the era boundaries (1492, 1776, 1865) as sharp natural breaks.
commonMistakes.correction: They are conventions historians chose. Change and continuity cross them, and Indigenous history in particular stretches far before and beyond any of these dates.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a side: either the founders' ideals were a lie, or the injustices do not really count.
commonMistakes.correction: Both the ideals and the injustices are historically real and coexisted. The honest task is to hold them together, not to cancel one with the other.

commonMistakes.mistake: Telling U.S. history as one group's story while others merely appear.
commonMistakes.correction: It was made by Native American, European, African, and immigrant peoples interacting; leaving any of them out distorts what actually happened.
That slavery was legal in 1776 is a fact; why the founders tolerated it, and what the Declaration ultimately meant, are interpretations open to reasoned debate.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging the past only by present standards (presentism) and stopping there.
commonMistakes.correction: Explain the historical context and name the harm accurately. Understanding why people acted and condemning injustice are not in conflict.

compareContrast.distinction: The ideals stated who ought to be free and equal; the realities showed who actually was. The gap between them drives much of U.S. history.
A fact (slavery was legal in 1776) is settled by evidence; an interpretation (what the Revolution ultimately meant) is argued from that evidence and can differ.
This lesson is the map of the whole arc; colonial-america, american-revolution, slavery, and civil-war are the detailed stops it hands off to.

keyTakeaway: U.S. history is a rough arc from Indigenous America to world power, made by diverse peoples, and its central thread is the honest, unresolved tension between the nation's founding ideals and the realities that denied them to millions.

questionBank.prompt: According to the lesson, the standard sequence of eras used to organize U.S. history (contact, colonization, founding, expansion and slavery, Civil War, industrialization, world power) should be understood as:
options: A useful but contestable convention rather than a fixed feature of the past
A precise natural timeline that all historians agree on
A list invented in 1776 by the authors of the Declaration
The only correct way to divide American history
questionBank.explanation: The lesson repeatedly frames periodization as a convenience historians choose, with contested boundaries, not a law of nature. The other options overstate its fixedness, misattribute its origin, or deny that the scheme is contestable.
questionBank.skill: Recalling that periodization is a convention

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best captures how the lesson says to handle the founding ideals of liberty and equality alongside the era's injustices?
options: Emphasize the ideals and treat the injustices as minor exceptions
Conclude that the ideals were meaningless because they were not honored
Hold both as historically real at once and treat the gap between them as a central subject
Avoid the ideals entirely and study only the injustices
questionBank.explanation: The lesson insists the honest move is to hold the ideals and the injustices together, since both are true, and to treat the distance between them as one of U.S. history's main subjects. The other options each drop or cancel one side.

questionBank.prompt: A student writes: 'The Declaration of Independence proves that the United States guaranteed equality to everyone in 1776.' Using the lesson's approach, the strongest correction is that:
options: The Declaration was not written until the 1860s, so the date is wrong
Equality was fully guaranteed, so the sentence is essentially correct
The Declaration was about trade policy, not rights, so equality is irrelevant
The Declaration stated an ideal of equality that the society did not extend to enslaved people, women, and Native nations at the time
questionBank.explanation: Historical thinking distinguishes the Declaration's aspiration ('created equal') from the reality that slavery was legal and women and Native peoples were excluded. Option A is factually false (1776), B ignores documented exclusions, and C misdescribes the document.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing an ideal from the historical reality

questionBank.prompt: You encounter a firsthand account praising an 1830 policy that removed a Native nation from its land. Applying the lesson's historical-thinking skills, your best first step is to:
options: Accept it as settled fact because it is a firsthand account
Ask who wrote it and why, and compare it with other sources including the removed nation's perspective
Reject it entirely because it is old and therefore unreliable
Treat its praise of the policy as proof the policy was just
questionBank.explanation: Sourcing and corroboration mean asking about the author's purpose and comparing multiple perspectives, including the dispossessed nation's. Being firsthand does not make it neutral (A, D), and age alone does not make a source worthless (C).
questionBank.skill: Applying sourcing and corroboration to a source

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following is an established fact rather than an interpretation, as the lesson uses those terms?
options: The American Revolution was ultimately a triumph for human freedom
The founders would have ended slavery if they had lived longer
Slavery was legal in the new United States and the enslaved population grew to nearly four million by 1860
The Declaration's ideals were the most important cause of later reform movements
questionBank.explanation: That slavery was legal and that the enslaved population reached nearly four million by 1860 is settled by census evidence. The other options are interpretive judgments about meaning, motive, or causal weight that historians could reasonably debate.

provenance.rightsStatus: Reference-only sources (OpenStax U.S. History OER; SHEG/Digital Inquiry Group; OER Project) plus public-domain U.S. government texts (Declaration of Independence and NARA census compilation). All wording original; only short exact quotations of the public-domain Declaration are reproduced, with attribution.
provenance.transformation: The framing arc, the ideals-vs-realities tension, the multi-peoples account, and the historical-thinking method were synthesized from the sources and written in original prose. The Declaration's exact phrases and date were verified against the National Archives transcript; the enslaved-population figures (~700,000 in 1790; nearly four million by 1860) are the standard federal census counts, corroborated across sources and stated as rounded approximations. Specific U.S. eras are named only as handoffs to sibling topics.
